entries.name: commit
entries.title: Conventional Commit
entries.description: Looks at the staged changes and writes a single conventional-commit message.
entries.author: DevFlow
entries.content:
description: Write a conventional commit for the staged changes
Look at the staged changes with `git diff --cached` and write a single conventional-commit message.

Format: `type(scope): summary` where type is one of feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore.
The summary is imperative, present tense, max 72 characters, no trailing period.
Reply with the message only — ready to paste into `git commit -m`.

entries.name: code-review
entries.title: Senior Code Review
entries.description: Reviews the working-tree diff and reports findings by severity.
entries.author: DevFlow
entries.content:
description: Review the working-tree diff and report findings by severity
Run `git diff` (and `git diff --cached` if staged changes exist) and review the changes like a senior engineer.

Report findings grouped by severity — P0 blocker, P1 should-fix, P2 nit — each with the file, the reasoning,
and a concrete suggested fix. End with a one-line verdict: approve, approve-with-comments, or request-changes.

entries.name: changelog
entries.title: Changelog Entry
entries.description: Turns the last commits into a tidy Keep-a-Changelog entry.
entries.author: DevFlow catalog
entries.content:
description: Write a Keep-a-Changelog entry from recent commits
Run `git log --oneline -15` and write ONE changelog entry in Keep a Changelog style.

Output only the markdown list items (Added/Changed/Fixed sub-sections where fitting), terse,
user-facing (no file lists), max 6 bullets. Match the tone of existing CHANGELOG.md entries if present.

entries.name: tdd
entries.title: Test-First Implement
entries.description: Implements a task strictly test-first (red → green → refactor).
entries.author: DevFlow catalog
entries.content:
description: Implement the task strictly test-first
For the requested change: 1) write a failing test that captures the behavior, 2) run it to confirm RED,
3) implement the minimal code to pass, 4) run the full suite to confirm GREEN, 5) refactor only if needed.
Never modify a test to make it pass unless the test itself encodes outdated behavior — say so explicitly.
